But psychological comfort and mental discipline aren't enough on their own. You can't just meditate your way through a financial crisis. You need a structural mechanical defense mechanism built into your portfolio.
Which brings us to the margin of safety. I want you to picture a loan officer at a commercial bank reviewing a borrower's file for a massive loan. The first level officer looks at the

income projections and asks, "Will this business pay us back our principle in interest if the economy stays good and they keep hitting their sales targets?" Seems reasonable. But the second level officer looks at the exact same file and asks, "What if a recession

hits tomorrow? and they lose their biggest client. What is the liquidation value of their factory equipment? Are there salailable assets to fall back on to recover our capital if everything goes absolutely wrong?
That is the essence of defensive investing and the margin of safety. What this means for you is that investing isn't about predicting sunny days and writing the momentum of a growing economy.
No, it is about actively preparing for worst case outcomes rather than blindly betting on probable ones.
It's about building a portfolio architecture that survives whatever reality actually arrives, even if it's a reality you completely failed to forecast.
